q: A new feline holding wing is comparing ventilation targets. What is the ASV standard for room air exchange and composition in animal housing?
o: 8 to 12 ACH with up to 30% recirculated air
10 to 20 room air exchanges per hour with fresh air
20 to 25 ACH with mandatory facility-wide HEPA
5 to 10 ACH with industrial ozone generators
e: ASV 2022 sets 10 to 20 room air exchanges per hour with fresh, non-recirculated air.

q: Fractious cats are housed so staff must use squeeze boards and feral dens forcefully every morning to clean. How is this categorized?
o: Acceptable if length of stay is under 7 days
Conditionally acceptable with Level 2 PPE
Unacceptable to house animals where daily care requires forceful handling equipment
Recommended, as it optimizes biosecurity
e: ASV: it is unacceptable to house animals in enclosures that require forceful handling equipment for daily care; use multi-compartment touch-free housing.

q: During a surge, staff house four friendly healthy dogs in an admin hallway and a restroom. Which is true?
o: Acceptable because the dogs are friendly and low risk
Unacceptable; except for a brief emergency, housing in spaces not intended for housing is forbidden
Acceptable if vaccinated and dewormed within 2 hours
Acceptable with a temporary visual barrier
e: ASV: except for brief emergencies, housing animals in spaces not intended for housing (bathrooms, hallways) is unacceptable.

q: What are the minimum and ideal individual floor-space figures for an adult cat?
o: Under 6 sq ft (0.6 sq m) is fine for short stays
Under 8 sq ft (0.75 sq m) is unacceptable; 11 sq ft (1.0 sq m) or more is ideal
Exactly 4 sq ft (0.4 sq m) regardless of stay
16 to 18 sq ft (1.5 to 1.7 sq m) minimum for any individual cat
e: ASV: individual adult cat housing under 8 sq ft (0.75 sq m) is unacceptable; 11 sq ft (1.0 sq m) or more is ideal.

q: For a group cohousing room of healthy adult cats, what is the minimum floor space per cat and the maximum number of adult cats?
o: 8 sq ft (0.75 sq m) per cat; maximum 12 cats
12 sq ft (1.1 sq m) per cat; maximum 10 cats
18 sq ft (1.7 sq m) per cat; maximum 6 adult cats
25 sq ft (2.3 sq m) per cat; maximum 4 cats
e: ASV: minimum 18 sq ft (1.7 sq m) per adult cat, and no more than six adult cats per enclosure (corrected from a draft 6 to 8).

q: A row of single-sided kennels holds alert, healthy dogs. Which practice is a critical welfare violation that must be halted?
o: Walking the dogs out during cleaning
Placing a dog on a secure tie-out in front of its pen while scrubbing
Hosing the kennel floors and walls while dogs remain inside
Restocking cleaning supplies weekly from central storage
e: Dogs must never be hosed down while inside the enclosure; remove animals from areas where overspray and stress occur.

q: To prevent droplet transmission when cats sneeze, what is the minimum spacing required between opposing rows of cat cages that face each other?
o: Greater than 2 ft (0.6 m)
Greater than 3 ft (0.9 m)
Greater than 4 ft (1.2 m)
Greater than 6 ft (1.8 m)
e: ASV: cat cages should face away or be spaced more than 4 ft (1.2 m) apart to prevent respiratory droplet transmission.

q: A draft proposes 4 ft (1.2 m) wide by 16 ft (4.9 m) long dog runs; the consultant recommends 8 ft (2.4 m) by 8 ft (2.4 m). What metric supports housing wider than 4 ft (1.2 m)?
o: It raises room temperature from 60 to 80 F (15.6 to 26.7°C) automatically
It maximizes ceiling-vent air velocity
It minimizes a dog's nose and tail hitting the side walls when turning
It removes the need for a double-compartment door
e: Design guidance: housing wider than 4 ft (1.2 m) prevents the nose and tail from hitting walls as the dog turns.

q: How should a large shelter structurally segregate its isolation wing to avoid coinfections?
o: One open ward with a central exhaust pulling air across all species
Separate isolation areas by syndrome and species (for example dermatology, respiratory, gastrointestinal)
Housing contagious animals in admin offices for observation
Shared indoor/outdoor runs with interconnected drainage
e: ASV requires species separation and separate areas for different contagious diseases; the textbook operationalizes this as syndrome-grouped rooms.

q: A shelter weighs reactivating overnight public drop boxes. How are drop boxes classified?
o: Highly recommended for 24-hour access
Conditionally acceptable with internal video monitoring
Entirely unacceptable due to safety risks, suffering, pathogen exposure, or death
Acceptable for adult cats if kept at 65 to 80 F (18.3 to 26.7°C)
e: ASV: unmonitored drop boxes are unacceptable; use on-call numbers, police drop-off, or vet ER agreements instead.

q: Which design choice best reduces chronic stress, frustration, and barking in a canine adoption ward?
o: Direct face-to-face room alignment for constant visual stimulation
Open warehouse housing with chain-link throughout
Enclosed individual rooms, walls continuous to the ceiling, laminated glass doors with a sniff hole
Plexiglass doors with no openings to isolate dogs from airflow cues
e: Enclosed rooms with continuous walls and laminated glass plus a sniff hole reduce noise transmission; note they then need mechanical ventilation.

q: What are the absolute prerequisites for a cat before entering a cohousing group?
o: Length of stay over 14 days and an indoor-only history
Individual health and behavior assessment, free of contagious disease signs, and negative FeLV and FIV
Mandatory 30-day quarantine regardless of exam
Documentation that the cat is over 10 years old
e: ASV: assess health and behavior, confirm freedom from contagious disease, and require negative FeLV and FIV before group entry.

q: For a heavy-duty wash-down run with daily heated water and disinfectants, which flooring is explicitly unacceptable?
o: Fluid-applied resinous epoxy or urethane
Polished sealed concrete
Paint, epoxy paint, wood, or vinyl
Slip-resistant porcelain tile with minimal grout
e: Paint, epoxy paint, wood, and vinyl cannot withstand industrial sanitation and are unacceptable for shelter floors.

q: What are the primary drawbacks of indoor/outdoor kennel units with guillotine doors?
o: Banned outright under ASV guidelines
Costly to build, waste energy, can freeze shut in cold climates, and trap humidity and mold in hot humid climates
They increase stereotypies versus small single rooms
They prevent any fresh-air ventilation system
e: Indoor/outdoor units are ideal for welfare but costly, energy-hungry, prone to freezing shut, and to humidity and mold in hot climates.

q: What is the correct directional workflow for daily cleaning and husbandry to limit fomite transmission?
o: Least healthy to healthiest (isolation to intake to adoption)
Storage to isolation to public lobby
Healthiest to least healthy (adoption to intake to isolation)
All dog pods first, felines left until evening
e: Begin with the healthiest and most susceptible and finish with the least healthy: adoption toward isolation.

q: On a restricted budget, which lighting strategy meets sustainability goals without harming circadian welfare?
o: High-intensity lights on 24 hours to prevent shedding
Removing all windows to stabilize heat transfer
Limit loads to under 1 watt per sq ft and use photosensors to dim lights near windows when daylight suffices
Legacy un-ballasted fluorescent fixtures only
e: Keep lighting under 1 W per sq ft and use photosensors near windows; preserve natural light for circadian rhythm.

q: In the needs-assessment process, what is the objective of developing the animal intake profile (Step 3)?
o: Track the volunteer-to-staff payroll ratio
Designate intake by mode of entry and animal type monthly for at least 2 years to optimize C4C and prevent over- or under-building
Map the ratio of urethane to tile grout
Eliminate all double-compartment enclosures
e: Step 3 records intake by mode and type monthly for at least 2 years to size housing to real demand and protect Capacity for Care.

q: Can a litter of four 8-week-old puppies be cohoused with three unrelated 10-week-old strays?
o: Yes, mixing unrelated puppies under 5 months maximizes socialization
Yes, with a prophylactic NSAID protocol
No; puppies and kittens under 20 weeks should not be cohoused with unfamiliar animals unless benefits clearly outweigh risks
No; pediatrics cannot be cohoused until spayed or neutered
e: ASV: under 20 weeks, do not cohouse with unfamiliar animals unless benefits outweigh risks due to infectious-disease susceptibility.

q: How is feline upper respiratory infection most effectively managed through infrastructure?
o: Convert feline rooms to outdoor wire cages for airflow
Through proper shelter design and air systems plus appropriate management, even with few isolation rooms
Lower exhaust vents to floor level by the public entrance
Increase group rooms to over 12 cats for herd immunity
e: FURI is best controlled by design, air systems, and management policies, not by crowding or exposure-increasing fixes.

q: Where should exhaust vents be positioned in a feline intake ward to minimize air cross-contamination?
o: Centrally on the ceiling over the hallway
At the rear of individual cat units
Low to the floor by the room's front door
Omitted to preserve a tight humidity zone
e: Place exhaust at the rear of individual cat units to reduce air cross-contamination between animals.

q: In the facility space-usage mix, what share goes to Animal Areas, and which sub-category is largest?
o: Public/Support 35%; Lobby 11% largest
Animal Areas 65%; Animal Housing 45% largest
Animal Areas 65%; Training 15% largest
Medical 5%; Support 7% largest
e: Animal Areas are about 65% of the building, with Animal Housing the single largest share at about 45%.

q: Why are off-centre drains recommended in a primary canine enclosure floor?
o: They raise ventilation from 10 to 20 ACH
They keep a dry space for the dog to rest while the floor finishes drying
They enable continuous pacing without wet paws
They remove the need for coved wall-floor junctions
e: Off-centre drains leave a dry resting area for the dog while wash-down water drains away.

q: On a tight retrofit budget, which filtration standard is sufficient for standard shelter HVAC units?
o: Industrial HEPA across all spaces
A pleated MERV 6 or 8 filter
Remove all filters if using barred doors
Activated carbon beds in feline zones only
e: MERV 6 or 8 pleated filters suffice for retrofits; HEPA is reserved for surgery. Filtration is an adjunct, not the sole control.

q: How should a highly fearful stray cat be transported and placed to optimize security?
o: Open wire crate at floor level past dog runs
Hand-carried by several volunteers for fast acclimation
Covered carrier or trap so it feels hidden, then transferred quickly to the highest available cage
Straight into a group room with 6 to 8 cats
e: Use covered carriers or traps and transfer to the highest available cage, consistent with the feline preference for elevation.

q: Which materials are explicitly unacceptable for shelter walls in a high-moisture, high-impact zone?
o: Solid surfaces and laminated glass
Sealed hard-trowelled cement plaster
Wood, painted wallboard, vinyl wall coverings, and standard concrete block
Polished-face block or large porcelain tile
e: Unacceptable walls: wood, painted wallboard, vinyl wall coverings, and standard concrete block.

q: What is the maximum number of adult dogs cohoused in one primary enclosure, and the preferred arrangement?
o: No more than 2 dogs under any circumstance
No more than 4 adult dogs, ideally paired
Up to 6 if all under 20 weeks from different sources
Up to 8 if fed from one communal bowl
e: ASV: two to four adult dogs per enclosure, with pairs preferred for safety and biosecurity.

q: What behavioral changes were documented when shelter dogs were given 9 sq m (97 sq ft) or larger pens?
o: More fence-pacing and vocalization
Increased general activity and visual exploration, less stereotypy, and more positive interactions
Ceased all vocalization and needed no walks
Preferred single-compartment stainless housing
e: Dogs in 9 sq m (97 sq ft) or larger pens showed more activity and exploration, less stereotypy, and more positive interactions.

q: Where should surgery and recovery rooms sit relative to other zones?
o: Inside the public lobby to showcase operations
At a distance from isolation areas but close to animal housing to minimize patient movement
Connected to the intake sally port to save space
Inside the feline cohousing room for a home-like recovery
e: Place surgery and recovery away from isolation yet near housing to minimize transport of surgical patients.

q: Why must a feline litter box accommodate the cat's entire body?
o: So 4 kittens from different litters can share it
To help the HVAC reach 10 to 20 ACH
Because a too-small box harms welfare and can cause house soiling
To remove the need for a connecting portal
e: ASV: the litter box must fit the whole body and allow posturing; too small harms welfare and risks house soiling.

q: For cats that fight at the moment of initial introduction, what is the documented long-term risk?
o: 10 times more likely to have panleukopenia vaccine failure
Nearly 40 times more likely to keep fighting in following weeks and months
Automatically a length of stay under 5 days
50 times more likely to guard elevated perches
e: Cats that fight at introduction are nearly 40 times more likely to continue fighting later, a strong signal to separate.

q: ASV cautions that attention to ventilation and air quality will NOT overcome which problems?
o: Inadequate housing, poor sanitation, or lax population management
Seasonal shedding and coat changes
Staff scheduling conflicts
High adoption demand
e: ASV: good air quality cannot compensate for inadequate housing, poor sanitation, or lax population management.

q: Capacity for Care (C4C) is best described as:
o: The number of cages physically present in the building
The maximum animals a shelter can house while still meeting each animal's full standard of care
The annual live release rate
The square footage of the medical suite
e: C4C is a welfare ceiling: the most animals that can be housed while still meeting the full standard of care, not a raw cage count.

q: How must isolation rooms relate to the rest of the housing, and what supports PPE use?
o: Open directly into the nearest ward for quick access
Not open directly into another housing area; use a corridor or vestibule that also serves for donning and doffing PPE
Share an open doorway with intake to speed transfers
Connect to the lobby for public viewing
e: ASV: isolation must not open directly into another housing area; a corridor or vestibule provides separation and a PPE space.

q: Where should animal intake occur within the facility?
o: In the busiest part of the public lobby
In a designated quiet space away from the main foot traffic, with elevated surfaces for carriers
In the surgery suite to centralize handling
In the isolation corridor
e: ASV: intake should occur in a quiet space away from foot traffic, with elevated surfaces to keep carriers off the floor.

q: Why are smaller cohousing spaces that allow an all-in/all-out approach advantageous?
o: They permit constant addition of new animals
They let enclosures be fully sanitized between groups and eliminate repeated new-introduction risk
They remove the need for monitoring
They allow more than six cats safely
e: All-in/all-out lets the space be sanitized between groups and avoids the stress and disease risk of repeated introductions.
